questions.stem: In the 4×4 gridworld of Example 4.1 (reward $-1$ per move, $\gamma = 1$) the equiprobable random policy has $v_\pi(11) = -14$ and terminal value 0. Moving down from state 11 reaches the terminal state; moving down from state 7 reaches state 11. Find $q_\pi(11, \text{down})$ and $q_\pi(7, \text{down})$.
solution: For a deterministic move, $q_\pi(s, a) = r + \gamma v_\pi(s')$.
$q_\pi(11, \text{down}) = -1 + 1 \cdot v_\pi(\text{terminal}) = -1 + 0 = -1$.
questions.explanation: An action value is one step of reward plus the value of the state you land in. After that step the policy π takes over.

misconceptions.why: That is v_π(11), the average over all four actions. Choosing down terminates immediately.

questions.stem: Run two-array iterative policy evaluation (4.5) on the 4×4 gridworld from $v_0 = 0$. After one sweep every nonterminal state has $v_1 = -1$. Compute the exact values $v_2(1)$ and $v_2(6)$. State 1 neighbours the terminal state on its left; state 6 has nonterminal neighbours 2, 5, 7 and 10.
solution: $v_2(s) = -1 + \tfrac14 \sum_{\text{4 moves}} v_1(s')$.
State 1: the moves lead to the terminal state (0), state 1 itself (up, off the grid: $-1$), state 2 ($-1$) and state 5 ($-1$). So $v_2(1) = -1 + \tfrac14(0 - 3) = -1.75$.
State 6: all four successors have $v_1 = -1$, so $v_2(6) = -1 + \tfrac14(-4) = -2$.
questions.explanation: Figure 4.2 prints $v_2(1)$ as −1.7. The exact value is −1.75 (see the figure-rounding flag on Example 4.1).

misconceptions.why: That is the printed one-decimal value. The exact two-array iterate is −1.75.

questions.stem: Put the steps of one pass of in-place iterative policy evaluation (Figure 4.1) in order.
options: For the next state $s$, remember $v \leftarrow V(s)$
Replace $V(s)$ by its full backup $\sum_a \pi(a|s)\sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a)[r + \gamma V(s')]$
After all states, stop if $\Delta < \theta$; otherwise start another sweep
solution: Reset the largest-change tracker at the start of each sweep.
For each state: save the old value, back it up in place, record the change.
Test the stopping condition once the sweep is complete.
questions.explanation: The old value must be saved before the backup overwrites it, or the change Δ cannot be measured.

questions.stem: In the 4×4 gridworld of Example 4.1 (equiprobable random policy, reward $-1$ per move, $\gamma = 1$), $v_\pi(12) = -22$, $v_\pi(13) = -20$ and $v_\pi(14) = -14$. A new state 15 is added below state 13. From 15, the moves left, up, right and down lead to 12, 13, 14 and 15. (i) If all the original transitions are unchanged, what is $v_\pi(15)$? (ii) If, in addition, moving down from 13 now leads to 15, what is $v_\pi(15)$?
solution: (i) No original state can reach 15, so their values stay as in Figure 4.2. The Bellman equation at 15: $v = -1 + \tfrac14(-22 - 20 - 14 + v)$.

(ii) Now 13's down move leads to 15 instead of back to 13. Try the values from (i): 13's equation used to contain $v(13) = -20$ for its down move, and now contains $v(15) = -20$. These are the same number, so every equation still holds.
$v_\pi$ is the unique solution of its Bellman equations, so the values are unchanged and $v_\pi(15) = -20$ again.
questions.explanation: This is Exercise 4.2 of the draft, reworded. The app solves both versions of the extended gridworld numerically (check ch04-q004). The second part works because state 15 turns out to have exactly the value of state 13.

misconceptions.why: The change only swaps one successor value $-20$ for another $-20$, so the solution of the equations does not move.

questions.stem: Continue two-array iterative policy evaluation (4.5) on the 4×4 gridworld. From $v_2$, where states 1, 4, 11 and 14 have $-1.75$ and every other nonterminal state has $-2$, compute the exact values $v_3(1)$ and $v_3(5)$. State 5's neighbours are 1 (up), 9 (down), 6 (right) and 4 (left).
solution: $v_3(s) = -1 + \tfrac14 \sum_{\text{4 moves}} v_2(s')$.
State 1: the moves lead to the terminal state (0), state 1 itself (up, off the grid: $-1.75$), state 2 ($-2$) and state 5 ($-2$). So $v_3(1) = -1 + \tfrac14(-5.75) = -2.4375$.
questions.explanation: Figure 4.2 prints these values as $-2.4$ and $-2.9$. Under ordinary rounding, $-2.875$ to one decimal would also be $-2.9$, and $-2.4375$ would be $-2.4$ (see the figure-rounding flag on Example 4.1).

questions.stem: How does the in-place version of iterative policy evaluation (Figure 4.1) differ from the two-array version of (4.5)?
options: Each backed-up value immediately replaces the old one, so later backups in the same sweep may use new values; it also converges to $v_\pi$, usually faster
Only the two-array version converges to $v_\pi$
The in-place version needs one array for old values and one for new values
In the in-place version the order in which states are backed up makes no difference to the speed of convergence
optionNotes: Correct, as §4.1 describes. The app also checks that both versions reach the same $v_\pi$ (check ch04.in-place-converges-to-same-v).
The draft states that the in-place algorithm also converges to $v_\pi$.
It is the two-array version that keeps separate arrays for $v_k$ and $v_{k+1}$.
The draft says the sweep order strongly affects how quickly the in-place version converges.
solution: Two-array: compute all of $v_{k+1}$ from $v_k$, leaving $v_k$ untouched.
In-place: one array, where each backup overwrites its state's value, so later backups can use values already updated in this sweep.
Both converge to $v_\pi$. The in-place version usually converges faster, and its speed depends on the order of the sweep.
questions.explanation: The draft usually has the in-place version in mind when it discusses DP algorithms.

questions.stem: True or false: in general, iterative policy evaluation reaches $v_\pi$ exactly after a finite number of sweeps.
solution: The sequence $\{v_k\}$ converges to $v_\pi$ as $k \to \infty$: it is a limit.
In practice the algorithm is stopped once the largest change in a sweep falls below a small threshold $\theta$, leaving $V \approx v_\pi$.
questions.explanation: This is why Figure 4.1 outputs $V \approx v_\pi$ rather than $v_\pi$.

questions.stem: In Figure 4.1, $\Delta$ is set to 0 at the start of each sweep, and each backup does $\Delta \leftarrow \max(\Delta, |v - V(s)|)$. What does $\Delta$ hold when the test $\Delta < \theta$ is made?
options: The largest change made to any single state's value during the sweep just completed
The error $|V(s) - v_\pi(s)|$ at the last state backed up
The total change summed over all states in the sweep
The change made to the last state backed up
optionNotes: Correct: $\Delta$ is reset each sweep and takes the maximum over every backup in it.
$v_\pi$ is unknown, which is why it is being computed. $\Delta$ measures how much the values changed, not their distance from $v_\pi$.
The update takes a maximum, not a sum.
$\Delta$ keeps the largest change seen anywhere in the sweep, not only the last one.
solution: At the start of a sweep $\Delta = 0$.
After each state's backup, $\Delta$ becomes the larger of itself and that state's change $|v - V(s)|$.
At the end of the sweep $\Delta = \max_s |\text{change at } s|$. This is the stopping test the draft describes.
questions.explanation: A small $\Delta$ means the values have nearly stopped changing. It is a practical stopping rule, not a certificate of exact equality with $v_\pi$.

verification.note: Figure 4.1 and the stopping rule, printed p. 92.

questions.stem: Run two-array value iteration (4.10) on the 4×4 gridworld (γ = 1) from $v_0 = 0$. After one sweep every nonterminal state has $v_1 = -1$. Compute $v_2(1)$ and $v_2(6)$.
solution: $v_2(s) = \max_a [-1 + v_1(s')]$, with $v_1 = 0$ at the terminal states and $-1$ elsewhere.
State 1 can move left into the terminal state: $v_2(1) = -1 + 0 = -1$.
State 6 has only nonterminal neighbours: $v_2(6) = -1 + (-1) = -2$.
questions.explanation: Compare $v_2(1) = -1.75$ under policy evaluation of the random policy: the max picks the best move instead of averaging over all four.

misconceptions.why: That is the policy-evaluation value, which averages over the random policy's moves. Value iteration takes the maximum.

questions.stem: Solve the gambler's problem (Example 4.3) with $p_h = 0.4$ by value iteration. What are $v_*(25)$ and $v_*(50)$, the optimal probabilities of reaching a capital of 100 from capital 25 and from capital 50?
solution: From capital 50, staking everything wins with probability $p_h = 0.4$, and no strategy does better when $p_h < \tfrac12$.
From capital 25, staking 25 reaches capital 50 with probability 0.4, and from there the best is 0.4 again: $v_*(25) = 0.4 \cdot 0.4 = 0.16$.
Value iteration converges to these values (Figure 4.6).
questions.explanation: With an unfavourable coin, bold play maximises the chance of reaching the goal, so these are the values of bold play.

questions.stem: Why does policy iteration on a finite MDP reach an optimal policy after finitely many iterations?
options: There are finitely many deterministic policies, and each improvement is strict unless the policy is already optimal
Each policy evaluation is exact after one sweep
The discount factor γ < 1 forces the values to shrink each iteration
The value function changes by less than θ after each improvement
optionNotes: Correct: strict improvement plus a finite set of policies means the process cannot go on for ever.
Evaluation is itself iterative and usually needs many sweeps.
The argument does not depend on γ < 1; the gridworld example uses γ = 1.
θ controls when an evaluation stops, not how many improvements are needed.
solution: Each improvement step gives a strictly better policy unless the current one is already optimal (the policy improvement theorem).
A finite MDP has only finitely many deterministic policies, so no policy can repeat and the sequence must end at an optimal one.
questions.explanation: The draft gives this argument on p. 97. The Figure 4.3 pseudocode can still cycle between equally good policies, which the draft acknowledges.

verification.note: The finite-convergence argument, printed p. 97, checked against the text layer.

questions.stem: Run policy iteration on the 4×4 gridworld (γ = 1), starting from the equiprobable random policy. After the first improvement the policy is greedy with respect to $v_{\text{random}}$. What are $v_{\pi_1}(1)$ and $v_{\pi_1}(6)$ for that improved policy? State 1 is next to the top-left terminal corner; state 6 is in row 1, column 2.
solution: $v_{\text{random}}$ (Figure 4.2) increases towards the two terminal corners, so the greedy policy moves each state along a shortest path to a corner.
Every move costs −1, so $v_{\pi_1}(s)$ is minus the number of moves to the nearer corner.
State 1 is one move from the corner: $v_{\pi_1}(1) = -1$. State 6 is three moves from either corner: $v_{\pi_1}(6) = -3$.
questions.explanation: On this problem one improvement already gives an optimal policy, as the draft notes for Figure 4.2.
